questions.question: Describe the three structural families for a transportable shelter with the engineering behind each, and explain how two ideas are sketched with dimensions, materials, joints, cover and floor.
questions.expected_answer: The dome, from the hoop tent and the beehive hut, uses bent rods pushed into the ground or a base ring and tied to each other and to hoops so every member is in compression along its length or tension round a ring and none bends; it is light, strong in wind from any direction, beamless and quick, but needs rods that bend without breaking and a cover cut to the curve. The ridge or A-frame, from the classic tent, has two A-shaped ends joined by a ridge pole with the cover pegged out, triangulated by its shape; it is simple with flat-sheet covers and straight poles and good headroom along the ridge, but catches wind on its ends and needs guy ropes. The frame or box, from the gazebo and prefabricated unit, is a rectangular pole frame with a pitched roof braced by diagonals; it gives the most room but is heaviest and slowest and every rectangle must be triangulated. Two ideas are sketched on a folded page in 3D or side and end views, freehand and labelled, with dimensions proving 21 square metres and 1.8 metres headroom, such as a 5.2 metre dome or a 4 by 5.3 metre ridge or box; frame material and section are stated, 16 millimetre fibreglass or conduit rods for a dome, 32 millimetre steel tube or 50 millimetre timber for ridge or box, with joints as sleeves, lashings or pins; the cover of the specified textile is drawn fixed by eyelets at 500 millimetre spacing, a pegged or tucked hem, overlaps laid for runoff and overhanging eaves, and the cheaper tarpaulin groundsheet turned up at the edges.

questions.question: List the features that must be labelled on the shelter sketch to meet the requirement and health and safety lists, including transport and erection, and explain the crediting of borrowed ideas.
questions.expected_answer: The door as an overlapping flap on the side away from the prevailing wind with ties inside and out; a hooded vent at the peak and a low vent on the opposite wall, each about 0.1 square metre with its rain hood; a marked stove place near the high vent and away from the walls on an iron sheet or slab, or an outdoor cooking area on the camp plan; a lamp hook at the peak; a translucent daylight strip; a storage pocket or low shelf. For wind, guy ropes at 45 degrees, the hem pegged every 500 millimetres, dome rod feet 300 millimetres into the ground or on a weighted ring, guys from ridge ends. For rain, a roof pitch of at least 30 degrees so water does not pool, overhanging eaves and the turned-up groundsheet. For fire, two metre spacing shown on a small camp plan. For privacy, an opaque cover, a door fastening inside and an internal curtain line. The packed form is drawn as a bundle of rods about 1.2 metres long, a rolled cover and a bag of pegs and ties, with an estimated mass under 25 kilograms, and six numbered erection steps with times totalling under an hour using only a mallet. Each borrowed feature is credited to its source, the dome to the hoop tent and beehive hut, the ridge to the canvas tent, triangulation to the crane and pylon, bottom-up overlaps and a roof net to Zulu thatch, the low door to the beehive hut, the courtyard to the Venda homestead and the turned-up floor to the matjieshuis mat, since the rubric rewards ideas traceable to the investigation.

questions.question: Explain how the sketched ideas are checked, tested with quick models and chosen, and what the final design product contains.
questions.expected_answer: A table lists every specification and safety requirement down the side with the ideas across, and each cell holds a tick, cross or question mark with a word of reason: the dome ticks space, wind, erection, transport, door and vents but questions edge headroom, a curved cover's seams, the stove place near a leaning wall and rod cost; the ridge ticks space, flat-sheet waterproofing, erection, transport, stove place and cost but crosses headroom for six and questions wind on its ends; the box ticks space, headroom, wind if triangulated and waterproofing but crosses erection time, transport and cost. The idea with the fewest crosses on the most important lines is chosen with reasons written as sentences, hybrids being allowed if their parents are named and they are drawn, and what the chosen idea must still solve is recorded. Each form is built in a minute from straws, string and tissue and pushed from the side and top, blown on and given a teaspoon of water on the roof; the untriangulated box folds, the ridge leans until guyed and the dome springs back, and these observations are noted and may change the choice. The chosen sketch is redrawn clean with all labels and dimensions, a camp plan showing spacing, water and toilet positions, the erection steps and the packed form, and filed as the design product from which the model is built and against which it is marked.
